title: Gestalt principles: how the eye groups things
summary: See why your eye groups things by spacing, looks, and shared boxes, and use it to make screens easy to scan.
objective: Group related items on a screen using closeness, matching looks, and shared containers.

hook.prompt: Look at these dots for a second. What do you see?

visual.html: <svg direction='ltr' viewBox='0 0 210 100' width='210' height='100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><g class='fill-primary'><circle cx='30' cy='20' r='6'/><circle cx='30' cy='40' r='6'/><circle cx='30' cy='60' r='6'/><circle cx='30' cy='80' r='6'/><circle cx='80' cy='20' r='6'/><circle cx='80' cy='40' r='6'/><circle cx='80' cy='60' r='6'/><circle cx='80' cy='80' r='6'/><circle cx='130' cy='20' r='6'/><circle cx='130' cy='40' r='6'/><circle cx='130' cy='60' r='6'/><circle cx='130' cy='80' r='6'/><circle cx='180' cy='20' r='6'/><circle cx='180' cy='40' r='6'/><circle cx='180' cy='60' r='6'/><circle cx='180' cy='80' r='6'/></g></svg>
visual.alt: Sixteen identical dots in four columns of four; dots within a column sit much closer together than the columns do.

options.feedback: Most people don't see rows here: the dots in each row are far apart, so they don't feel connected.

options.text: One even grid with no groups
options.feedback: The dots are identical, yet most people still see groups. Something besides the dots themselves is doing it.

hook.explanation: Nothing connects the dots, yet most people see four columns. The only cue is spacing. Why does that work?

bricks.title: Close together means together
bricks.body: Your eye sorts what it sees into groups before you read a word. The first rule is **proximity**: things placed close together look related, and things far apart look separate. Below, spacing alone splits identical dots into two groups. On a screen, that means a label should sit nearer its own field than the field above it, and related items need less space between them than unrelated ones.

term.definition: Things that are close together are seen as one group.

visual.html: <svg direction='ltr' viewBox='0 0 240 40' width='240' height='40' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><g class='fill-primary'><circle cx='20' cy='20' r='7'/><circle cx='42' cy='20' r='7'/><circle cx='64' cy='20' r='7'/><circle cx='132' cy='20' r='7'/><circle cx='154' cy='20' r='7'/><circle cx='176' cy='20' r='7'/><circle cx='198' cy='20' r='7'/><circle cx='220' cy='20' r='7'/></g></svg>
visual.alt: Eight identical dots in a line: three close together, a wide gap, then five close together.

bricks.prompt: Which form makes it clear which label belongs to which field?

visual.html: NameEmail
visual.alt: A form where the Email label sits exactly halfway between the Name field above and the Email field below.

options.feedback: Each label sits as close to the field above it as to its own, so the spacing doesn't say which field it names.

visual.html: NameEmail
visual.alt: A form where each label sits just above its own field, with a wide gap before the next label.

bricks.hint: Which label is clearly nearer its own field than the one above?
bricks.explanation: Here each label hugs its own field and a bigger gap separates the pairs, so proximity pairs every label with the right field.

bricks.prompt: A designer meant each price to sit under its mug's name, but the spacing came out like this. Which mug will shoppers think costs $24?

visual.html:
Blue mug

$24

Green mug

$18

Red mug

$12
visual.alt: A list: Blue mug, a wide gap, then $24 sitting right above Green mug, another wide gap, then $18 right above Red mug, a wide gap, and $12.

options.feedback: That's what the designer meant, but $24 sits far from Blue mug and right against Green mug, so the eye pairs it with Green mug.

options.text: Nobody: shoppers will read the list carefully
options.feedback: People scan before they read, and spacing groups things at a glance. Most will pair the price with the name it touches.

bricks.hint: Which name is the price closest to?
bricks.explanation: $24 is far from Blue mug and almost touching Green mug, so proximity groups it with Green mug, whatever the designer intended.

bricks.title: Look alike, belong together
bricks.body: The second rule is **similarity**: things that look alike, in color, shape, or size, seem to belong together, even when they're spread out. Below, every dot is evenly spaced, yet you see columns, because each column shares a color. On a screen, if every link is underlined, people treat anything underlined as a link, and text styled like a link will get clicked.

term.definition: Things that look alike are seen as one group.

visual.html: <svg direction='ltr' viewBox='0 0 160 100' width='160' height='100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><g class='fill-primary'><circle cx='20' cy='20' r='7'/><circle cx='20' cy='50' r='7'/><circle cx='20' cy='80' r='7'/><circle cx='100' cy='20' r='7'/><circle cx='100' cy='50' r='7'/><circle cx='100' cy='80' r='7'/></g><g class='fill-muted-foreground' opacity='0.45'><circle cx='60' cy='20' r='7'/><circle cx='60' cy='50' r='7'/><circle cx='60' cy='80' r='7'/><circle cx='140' cy='20' r='7'/><circle cx='140' cy='50' r='7'/><circle cx='140' cy='80' r='7'/></g></svg>
visual.alt: A grid of evenly spaced dots in four columns, with the columns alternating between dark and light dots.

bricks.prompt: In this footer, only Privacy and Terms are links. Tap the item people will wrongly try to click.

visual.html: PrivacyTermsOpen 9 to 5Made in Lisbon

bricks.hint: Which plain piece of text is dressed up like the links?
bricks.explanation: **Open 9 to 5** is styled exactly like the two links, so similarity groups it with them and people will tap it.

bricks.prompt: Which of these make scattered items look like one group through similarity?

options.text: Giving them the same icon shape

options.feedback: That groups them too, but through proximity, not similarity. Similarity is about how things look, not where they sit.
Alphabetical order only shows up once you read the words. Similarity works at a glance, through color, shape, or size.

bricks.hint: Similarity is about how things look.
bricks.explanation: Color, shape, and size are all ways things can look alike, so each one makes scattered items read as a set.

bricks.title: Same box, same group
bricks.body: The third rule is **common region**: things inside the same border or background look like one group. Below, the dots are evenly spaced, but the boxes pair them up. It's one of the strongest grouping cues, strong enough to outweigh closeness. That's why cards work: put related settings inside one card, and people read them as a set without being told.

term.definition: Things inside the same border or background are seen as one group.

visual.html: <svg direction='ltr' viewBox='0 0 260 50' width='260' height='50' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><g class='fill-muted stroke-border' stroke-width='1.5'><rect x='12' y='6' width='76' height='38' rx='10'/><rect x='92' y='6' width='76' height='38' rx='10'/><rect x='172' y='6' width='76' height='38' rx='10'/></g><g class='fill-primary'><circle cx='30' cy='25' r='7'/><circle cx='70' cy='25' r='7'/><circle cx='110' cy='25' r='7'/><circle cx='150' cy='25' r='7'/><circle cx='190' cy='25' r='7'/><circle cx='230' cy='25' r='7'/></g></svg>
visual.alt: Six evenly spaced dots in a line, with a rounded box drawn around each pair, making three pairs.

bricks.prompt: Match each design choice to the principle that makes it work.

pairs.left: A label sits just above its own field
Billing options sit inside their own card

bricks.hint: Ask what each one uses: space, looks, or a container.
bricks.explanation: The label relies on closeness, the links on looking alike, and the card on a shared container.

bricks.prompt: Which two dots look like a pair?

visual.html: <svg direction='ltr' viewBox='0 0 180 82' width='180' height='82' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect class='fill-muted stroke-border' stroke-width='1.5' x='40' y='10' width='100' height='40' rx='10'/><g class='fill-primary'><circle cx='26' cy='30' r='6'/><circle cx='52' cy='30' r='6'/><circle cx='128' cy='30' r='6'/><circle cx='154' cy='30' r='6'/></g><g class='fill-muted-foreground' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-family='system-ui, sans-serif'><text x='26' y='72'>1</text><text x='52' y='72'>2</text><text x='128' y='72'>3</text><text x='154' y='72'>4</text></g></svg>
visual.alt: Four numbered dots: dots 1 and 2 sit close together, as do dots 3 and 4, but one box encloses dots 2 and 3.

options.feedback: They are the closest, but dot 2 shares a box with dot 3. A shared box outweighs closeness.
They are close, but dot 3 sits inside the box with dot 2, and a shared container beats proximity.
Your eye always looks for groups. Here the box makes one pair stand out.

bricks.hint: Which grouping cue did the lesson call one of the strongest?
bricks.explanation: Dots 2 and 3 are farther apart than their neighbors, but the shared box groups them. Common region wins over proximity.

challenge.situation: Your checkout form lists **Shipping address** and **Billing address** fields in one long column, all evenly spaced. The two section headings look exactly like the field labels. Shoppers keep typing billing details into shipping fields.

options.text: Put each address in its own card with a larger, bolder heading, and keep each label close to its field
options.outcome: The cards split the form into two clear sets, the headings no longer pass for labels, and every label obviously owns its field.

options.text: Add a wide gap between the shipping fields and the billing fields
options.outcome: The gap splits the form in two, which helps. But the headings still look like labels, so many shoppers miss where billing starts.

options.text: Make every heading and label bold so they all stand out
options.outcome: Headings and labels still look alike, and the spacing is still even, so nothing tells shoppers where one address ends.

challenge.hint: Look for the fix that uses more than one grouping cue.
challenge.explanation: A card for each address (common region), headings that look different from labels (similarity), and tight label spacing (proximity) all point the same way.

takeaways: Put related things close together and unrelated things farther apart.
Style things that do the same job alike, and never style plain text like a link.
Use cards or shared backgrounds to group a set; a shared box beats closeness.
When something is grouped wrong, check spacing, looks, and containers first.
